stem: An electronic health record fails to display an expected allergy alert during medication ordering. Which organizational response best supports patient safety?

options.A: Investigate the clinical decision-support failure and continue systematic testing, monitoring, and improvement of EHR alerts and order-entry safeguards.
options.B: Disable all medication alerts permanently after this event because one missed warning shows that clinical decision support creates more risk than benefit.
options.C: Return immediately to paper-only ordering throughout the organization because an isolated EHR alert failure proves electronic ordering cannot be made safe.
options.D: Leave the system unchanged if no second failure occurs because clinical decision-support tools do not require ongoing monitoring after implementation.

rationale: ONC's 2025 SAFER CPOE with Decision Support guide identifies recommended safety practices for the design, implementation, use, and monitoring of orders, alerts, warnings and clinical decision support. ONC also emphasizes configuration, validation, maintenance, monitoring and improvement of health IT. A therefore addresses the failure as a safety signal requiring investigation and continued system improvement. B, C and D either abandon useful safeguards or ignore the need for ongoing monitoring.
educational_objective: Treat an EHR alert failure as a patient-safety signal requiring investigation, validation, monitoring, and improvement of clinical decision-support safeguards.

source_original.stem: An electronic health record fails to display an expected allergy alert during medication ordering. Which organizational response best supports patient safety?

options.A: Investigate the clinical decision-support failure and continue systematic testing, monitoring, and improvement of EHR alerts and order-entry safeguards.
options.B: Disable all medication alerts permanently after this event, because one missed warning shows that clinical decision support creates more risk than benefit.
options.C: Return immediately to paper-only ordering throughout the organization, because an isolated EHR alert failure proves electronic ordering cannot be made safe.
options.D: Leave the system unchanged if no second failure occurs, because clinical decision-support tools do not require ongoing monitoring after implementation.

source_original.rationale: An allergy-alert failure is a patient-safety signal that warrants investigation and ongoing evaluation of the clinical decision-support system. Option A matches ONC SAFER guidance on safe design, implementation, use, and monitoring of CPOE and CDS. Option B overreacts by disabling all alerts rather than correcting the failure. Option C abandons electronic ordering based on a single defect instead of improving the system. Option D ignores the need for ongoing monitoring after implementation.

correction_summary: No clinical correction required. Reverified the 2025 SAFER guide as the current ONC resource and tied the rationale to ONC's explicit design/implementation/use/monitoring language without asserting that any single remediation is universally required.

audit_findings.exact_locator: CPOE with Decision Support guide description and SAFER system-management/use guidance.
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final answer stays at investigation/testing/monitoring/improvement principle and does not invent a mandatory technical fix.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A supports resilient EHR safety management.
audit_findings.cueing: All choices are organizational responses to the same failure.
audit_findings.blueprint: Quality improvement/information technology under Management of Care.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Confirmed ONC currentness and avoided unsupported causal assumptions about why the alert failed.
